title: Redis: leaderboards, rate limiting & geo
seriesDescription: How to use Redis in system design interviews: the data model, durability limits, clustering, caching, distributed locks, leaderboards, rate limiting, geo search, streams and pub/sub, with the trade-offs interviewers probe.
description: Sorted sets for rankings, fixed and sliding window rate limiters, and geohash-backed proximity search.
source: Study notes: how to use Redis in system design interviews

questions.prompt: Which Redis structure suits a leaderboard of the most-liked posts?

options.text: A sorted set, scoring each member by its like count.
options.why: Right: rank queries are logarithmic.

options.text: A list, appending each like to the end.
options.why: A list has no ranking by score.

options.text: A hash from post id to like count, sorted by the client.
options.why: Sorting on the client defeats the point.

options.text: A pub/sub channel carrying like events.
options.why: Pub/Sub is not stored or ranked.

questions.explanation: ZADD sets or replaces a member's score, so re-adding a post with a new count moves its rank.

options.text: Only the top five posts by score.
options.why: Right: negative indexes count from the highest rank.

options.text: Only the lowest five posts by score.
options.why: It removes the lowest, keeping the top.

options.text: Everything except the single lowest post.
options.why: It removes ranks up to sixth from the top.

options.text: Nothing, because the range is invalid.
options.why: The range is valid and meaningful.

questions.explanation: Periodically trimming keeps the sorted set small.

questions.prompt: How does a fixed-window limiter work with INCR?

options.text: Increment a per-window counter; reject once the count exceeds N.
options.why: Right: simple and cheap.

options.text: Store each request in a list and count the list.
options.why: That is closer to a sliding window and costs more memory.

options.text: Delete the counter on every request.
options.why: Then the count would never grow.

options.text: Use pub/sub to broadcast request counts.
options.why: Pub/Sub is not a counter.

questions.explanation: Return 429, often with a Retry-After header.

questions.prompt: When should the window expiry be set in the fixed-window limiter?

options.text: Only when INCR returns 1, the first request of the window.
options.why: Right: otherwise traffic keeps pushing the reset forward.

options.text: On every request, to keep the key alive.
options.why: A steady stream would never see a fresh window.

options.text: Never, because Redis expires counters itself.
options.why: Without an expiry the counter never resets.

options.text: Only when the count exceeds N.
options.why: The window must start on the first request.

questions.explanation: Run INCR and EXPIRE as one Lua script so a crash between them cannot leave a counter that never resets.

questions.prompt: Select all steps of a sliding-window limiter using a sorted set per user.

options.text: Remove entries older than the window with ZREMRANGEBYSCORE.
options.why: Yes: drop expired timestamps.

options.text: Count what is left with ZCARD.
options.why: Yes: that is the current request count.

options.text: Add the new request with ZADD if the count is under N.
options.why: Yes: record accepted requests.

options.text: Delete the user's whole key after every request.
options.why: No: that would erase the history you need.

questions.explanation: Run the sequence as a Lua script so it executes atomically.

questions.prompt: Which commands add a point and search near a location?

options.text: GEOADD to index it and GEOSEARCH to query a radius.
options.why: Right: built-in geospatial support.

options.text: SADD and SMEMBERS on a set of coordinates in the majority of deployments.
options.why: Sets have no distance search.

options.text: XADD and XREAD on a stream of coordinates.
options.why: Streams are logs, not spatial indexes.

options.text: PUBLISH and SUBSCRIBE on a location channel as a general rule of thumb.
options.why: Pub/Sub does not store points.

questions.explanation: Under the hood, geo data is a sorted set keyed by geohash.

questions.prompt: Why does GEOSEARCH cost O(N + log M) with two different counts?

options.text: It first collects N candidates in grid-aligned boxes, then filters to the M within the exact radius.
options.why: Right: the boxes are imprecise.

options.text: It scans every key in the database twice for most everyday workloads under normal operating conditions.
options.why: It seeks into one sorted set.

options.text: It sorts all members on every query.
options.why: The set is already ordered by geohash.

options.text: It runs one query on each replica and merges them without any extra configuration in a typical production setup.
options.why: There is no such merge.

questions.explanation: Geohashes make a sorted-set seek possible; the second pass trims the bounding-box overshoot.

questions.prompt: True or false: sorted sets suit leaderboards partly because high write throughput and low read latency keep up where a SQL database starts to struggle.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: that is the practical advantage at scale.

options.text: False
options.why: It is a good fit at scale.

questions.explanation: Rank queries are logarithmic and the data lives in memory.

questions.prompt: Why wrap a multi-step rate limit check in a Lua script?

options.text: The whole script runs as one atomic command, so concurrent requests cannot interleave.
options.why: Right: no race between the steps.

options.text: Lua is required for any use of sorted sets as a general rule of thumb in the majority of deployments.
options.why: Sorted sets work with plain commands.

options.text: Lua scripts avoid network latency entirely without any extra configuration in a typical production setup.
options.why: The client still makes one round trip.

options.text: Lua scripts make the data durable.
options.why: Scripts do not change durability.

questions.explanation: Atomic scripts are the standard trick for lock release and rate limiting alike.
